---
title: "00 — Setup: your first proofs, and the loop"
---

> **Where you are.** This is the very first concept. By the end you'll have written three real proofs
> that Lean's kernel has *checked*, and you'll understand the cycle you'll repeat for the rest of the
> course. No prior Lean or logic is assumed. Take it slowly — every idea here comes back later.

## 1. What Lean actually is

Lean is two things fused into one program:

1. **A programming language** — you write functions, data types, recursion, much like any typed
   functional language (think Haskell or the typed core of Swift/Rust).
2. **A proof checker** — you state mathematical claims and write proofs of them, and Lean *mechanically
   verifies* that each proof is airtight.

The reason these can be the *same* system is the most important idea in the whole course, so we'll spend
real time on it in §3. For now, the practical consequence:

> **A tiny, trusted part of Lean — the *kernel* — has the final say.** Everything you write is
> ultimately reduced to something the kernel checks. If the kernel accepts it, it is correct. Not
> "looks correct," not "the author is confident" — *correct*, with the same finality as `2 + 2 = 4`.

This is why this course can be pure learn-by-doing with no human grader. You don't submit a proof and
wait for feedback. You either get the proof past the kernel (it compiles — we call that **green**) or
you don't (**red**). Green *is* the grade, and it is incorruptible. Our whole course leans on this: the
kernel is the **oracle**, and unlike a textbook's answer key, you cannot fudge it.

## 2. The pieces in front of you

This concept is a directory with four files. You'll see this same shape every time:

| File | What it is | You edit it? |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | the objective and "definition of done" | no |
| `explainer.qmd` | **this lesson** | no |
| `Skeleton.lean` | the theorems, with their proofs left as `sorry` + tips | **yes — this is your workspace** |
| `Solution.lean` | the finished, verified proofs (+ a couple of checks) | peek only when stuck |

The workflow is one command:

```bash
make lab C=00-foundations/00-setup
```

That asks Lean to check **your** `Skeleton.lean`. While any proof is missing, it's **red**; when you've
filled them all in correctly, it turns **green**. That red→green pulse is the heartbeat of the course.

## 3. The big idea: a proof is a program

Here is the insight that makes Lean work — *propositions-as-types*, also called the Curry–Howard
correspondence. Don't worry about the names; worry about the picture.

In an ordinary typed language you write things like `x : Nat` — "`x` is a value of type `Nat`." Lean
uses that *exact same* notation for proofs:

```lean
h : p
```

reads "`h` is a proof of the proposition `p`." A **proposition** (something that could be true or
false, like "`p` and `q`") is treated as a **type**, and a **proof** of it is a **value** (a term) of
that type. So:

- To *prove* a proposition = to *construct* a value of its type.
- "`p` is true" = "the type `p` has at least one value" (we can build a proof).
- "`p` is false-and-unprovable" = "the type `p` is empty" (no value can be built).

Why is this a good idea? Because now **building a proof is just programming**, and **checking a proof is
just type-checking** — something computers are extremely good at and we already trust. A proof of an
implication `p → q` is literally a *function* that turns a proof of `p` into a proof of `q`. A proof of
"`p` and `q`" is a *pair*: one proof of `p` alongside one proof of `q`. We'll see both right now.

(One technicality you can file away: propositions live in a special universe called `Prop`, where Lean
ignores *which* proof you built — any two proofs of the same proposition are interchangeable. That's the
difference between `Prop` and the data type `Nat`, where `2` and `3` are genuinely different. It won't
trip you up today.)

## 4. Your first proof, two ways: `and_swap`

The claim: *if `p` and `q` both hold, then `q` and `p` both hold.* In Lean:

```lean
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p := ...
```

Read the signature like a function declaration:

- `(p q : Prop)` — two arbitrary propositions (inputs).
- `(h : p ∧ q)` — a proof that *both* hold (another input). `∧` is "and."
- `: q ∧ p` — the thing we must produce (the output type / the goal).
- `:= ...` — the proof itself (the function body) goes here.

**What is `∧`, concretely?** In Lean, `p ∧ q` is a little structure with two fields: a proof of `p` and
a proof of `q`. You build one with the *anonymous constructor* `⟨_, _⟩` (type the brackets as `\<` and
`\>` in the editor), and you take it apart with `.1` (the first field) and `.2` (the second). So from
`h : p ∧ q` we have `h.1 : p` and `h.2 : q`.

### Term-mode proof (build the value directly)

```lean
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p := ⟨h.2, h.1⟩
```

That's the whole proof. We need a proof of `q ∧ p`, i.e. a pair `⟨proof of q, proof of p⟩`. We have
`h.2 : q` and `h.1 : p`, so `⟨h.2, h.1⟩` has exactly type `q ∧ p`. The kernel checks the types line up,
and accepts. A proof really is just a small data structure you assemble.

### Tactic-mode proof (build it interactively)

For anything bigger, writing the term directly is hard, so we usually build proofs *step by step* using
**tactics**, inside a `by` block. The same theorem:

```lean
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p := by
  constructor   -- goal `q ∧ p` splits into two goals: `q` and `p`
  · exact h.2   -- prove the `q` goal using h.2
  · exact h.1   -- prove the `p` goal using h.1
```

What's happening:

- `by` switches into tactic mode. Lean now shows you a **goal state**: the hypotheses you have (here
  `p q : Prop`, `h : p ∧ q`) above a line, and the goal (`⊢ q ∧ p`) below it. The turnstile `⊢` means
  "you must prove."
- `constructor` says "build the goal with its constructor." Since `q ∧ p` is built from a proof of `q`
  and a proof of `p`, this replaces one goal with **two**: `⊢ q` and `⊢ p`.
- The `·` bullets focus on one goal at a time. `exact h.2` says "the goal is *exactly* this term" — and
  `h.2 : q` matches `⊢ q`. Likewise `exact h.1` closes `⊢ p`.

Tactics don't produce a different kind of proof — behind the scenes they assemble the very same term
`⟨h.2, h.1⟩`. They're just a more convenient way to write it. **The single most important habit in
Lean:** in your editor, put the cursor at different points and *read the goal state*. It tells you
exactly what you have and what's left to prove.

## 5. When the computer can just check it: `two_plus_two`

Some claims are true simply because *both sides compute to the same thing*. The kernel can run
computations, so:

```lean
theorem two_plus_two : 2 + 2 = 4 := by rfl
```

`rfl` stands for *reflexivity*: it proves goals of the form `a = a`. But Lean checks equality **up to
computation** (the jargon is *definitional equality*): it evaluates `2 + 2`, gets `4`, sees `4 = 4`, and
accepts. You didn't reason about addition — you let the kernel *do* the addition. (This is the
"programming language" half of Lean earning its keep.)

A close cousin you'll use a lot is `decide`, which works for any claim Lean knows how to *decide* by a
terminating computation (equalities of concrete numbers, `≤` on numbers, etc.):

```lean
theorem two_plus_two' : 2 + 2 = 4 := by decide
```

Rule of thumb: if a goal is about *specific* values, try `rfl` or `decide` before reasoning by hand.

## 6. Your first induction: `zero_add'`

Now the interesting one. We'll prove `0 + n = n` for *every* natural number `n`. You might expect this
to be as free as `2 + 2 = 4`. It isn't — and *why* is genuinely illuminating.

Natural numbers in Lean are built from two constructors: `0` (zero) and `n + 1` (the successor of `n`).
Addition is *defined by recursion on its second argument*:

```lean
-- (this is how Nat.add is defined in Lean's core, paraphrased)
n + 0      = n                 -- base equation
n + (m+1)  = (n + m) + 1       -- step equation
```

Look carefully. The pattern-match is on the **second** argument:

- `n + 0 = n` is true *by definition* — the base equation says so directly. So `n + 0 = n` is provable
  by `rfl`, no work. Try it!
- `0 + n = n` is **not** one of the equations. To compute `0 + n` you must peel `n` apart, and `n` is a
  *variable* — the kernel can't peel an unknown. So `rfl` is stuck. We need **induction**: prove it for
  `0`, then prove that *if* it holds for `k` it holds for `k + 1`. Those two cases cover every natural
  number, because every natural number is reachable from `0` by repeatedly adding `1`.

This asymmetry (`add_zero` free, `zero_add` needs induction) surprises everyone the first time. It's not
a quirk — it's the shape of the definition showing through. Here's the proof:

```lean
theorem zero_add' (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero      => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, ih]
```

Walking through it with the goal state in mind:

- `induction n with` splits into the two cases above, named `zero` and `succ`.
- **Case `zero`** — goal `⊢ 0 + 0 = 0`. By the base equation `0 + 0` *is* `0`, so this is `rfl`.
- **Case `succ k ih`** — we're proving it for `k + 1`, and we get to *assume* it for `k`. That
  assumption is the **induction hypothesis** `ih : 0 + k = k`. The goal is `⊢ 0 + (k + 1) = k + 1`.
  - `rw [Nat.add_succ]` *rewrites* using the step equation `n + (m+1) = (n + m) + 1`. It finds
    `0 + (k + 1)` on the left and replaces it, turning the goal into `⊢ (0 + k) + 1 = k + 1`.
  - `rw [ih]` rewrites `0 + k` into `k` (that's what `ih` says), giving `⊢ k + 1 = k + 1`. `rw`
    automatically finishes a goal that has become `a = a`, so we're done.

`rw [a, b]` just does the rewrites left to right in sequence. And yes — `simp` or `omega` would have
closed this in one shot; we did it by hand on purpose, to *see* induction work. Throughout the course
we reach for the automatic tactics only after we understand what they're doing for us.

## 7. The loop in detail: `sorry`, red, and green

Open `Skeleton.lean`. Each proof is the placeholder `sorry`:

```lean
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p := by
  sorry
```

`sorry` is Lean's "trust me, I'll do it later" escape hatch — it lets a file compile with a *hole* where
a proof should be. That's dangerous (a `sorry` proves *anything*), so Lean always warns when one is
present. We turn that safety-net up to maximum: the first line of every skeleton is

```lean
set_option warningAsError true
```

which promotes the `sorry` warning to a hard **error**. So:

- Untouched skeleton → the `sorry`s are errors → `make lab` is **red**.
- You replace each `sorry` with a real proof → no warnings → it compiles → **green**.

When you're stuck, the error messages and the goal state are your guides. A few editor tools worth
knowing from day one (in VS Code with the Lean extension, the goal shows in the *Infoview* panel):

```lean
#check @and_swap     -- show the type/signature of something
#eval 2 + 2          -- run a computation and print the result (here: 4)
example : 0 + 5 = 5 := by exact?   -- ask Lean to search its library for a proof
```

`exact?`, `apply?`, and `rw?` are search tactics — when you don't know the next step, they suggest one.
`example` lets you state a throwaway goal to experiment without naming a theorem.

## 8. The honesty rule

Because `sorry` (and, separately, declaring your own `axiom`) can "prove" things by *assuming* them, we
guard against both. Every keystone proof is audited with:

```lean
#print axioms and_swap     -- ⇒ 'and_swap' does not depend on any axioms
#print axioms zero_add'    -- ⇒ 'zero_add'' does not depend on any axioms
```

`#print axioms T` lists every axiom `T` ultimately relies on. A finished proof here depends on *none*.
Some perfectly legitimate proofs later will list Lean's three accepted axioms — `propext`,
`Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` (roughly: propositions with the same truth-content are equal; you can
choose elements from non-empty sets; quotients behave well). Those are fine. The one thing that must
**never** appear is `sorryAx` — the fingerprint of a `sorry`. The command

```bash
make axioms
```

scans the whole course for stray `sorry`, ad-hoc `axiom`, and any `sorryAx` in a keystone, and fails if
it finds one. It is the precise, mechanical version of "never fudge the oracle."

## 9. Prove it

Open `Skeleton.lean`, replace each `sorry` with a real proof, and check with:

```bash
make lab C=00-foundations/00-setup
```

The three goals:

1. **`and_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p`** — swap a conjunction.
2. **`two_plus_two : 2 + 2 = 4`**.
3. **`zero_add' (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n`** — your first induction.

Try each one **cold** before reading on — that small struggle is where the learning is, and the skeleton
deliberately gives you nothing but the statement. Everything you need was built in §3–§8. If you get
stuck, §10 below has *graduated* hints (take the smallest that unblocks you), and `Solution.lean` has the
finished proofs — read those to understand *why*, never just to copy.

## 10. Hints for the skeleton

**`and_swap`.** You're handed a proof of `p ∧ q` and must produce one of `q ∧ p`.

- *Nudge:* §4 covered both halves of this — how to take a conjunction *apart*, and how to put one
  *together*. You only need to combine those two moves.
- *More:* a single term `⟨_, _⟩` does it; or in tactic mode, `constructor` then close each part with `exact`.

**`two_plus_two`.** This is about *specific* numbers, not a variable.

- *Nudge:* don't reason about addition at all — let the kernel compute both sides. Which one-word tactic
  from §5 does exactly that?

**`zero_add'`.** The variable `n` is precisely what blocks a direct `rfl`.

- *Nudge:* re-read §6 — it explains why `rfl` is stuck here, and which tactic to reach for instead.
- *More:* `induction n with | zero => ?_ | succ k ih => ?_` (each `?_` is a case for you to fill). The
  base case computes on its own; the step needs one rewrite by the `+`/successor step-equation, then the
  induction hypothesis `ih`.

## 11. Exercises (optional, for fluency)

Try these in a scratch file or by adding `example`s. They reinforce today's ideas:

1. Prove `or_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∨ q) : q ∨ p`. *Hint:* a proof of `∨` is built with `Or.inl` /
   `Or.inr`, and taken apart with `cases h with | inl hp => ... | inr hq => ...`. (Unlike `∧`, you must
   handle *both* ways the "or" could have been made.)
2. Prove `add_zero' (n : Nat) : n + 0 = n`. *Hint:* recall §6 — which side is the definition?
   How short can the proof be?
3. Prove `succ_eq (n : Nat) : n + 1 = Nat.succ n`. *Hint:* `rfl` may already work — why?

## 12. Corrections to the optional exercises

Work them yourself first — then check. Each is explained, not just dropped.

### Exercise 1 — `or_swap`

```lean
theorem or_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∨ q) : q ∨ p := by
  cases h with
  | inl hp => exact Or.inr hp
  | inr hq => exact Or.inl hq
```

The contrast with `and_swap` is the whole point. A proof of `p ∧ q` carries *both* a `p` and a `q`, so
in §4 we just reached in with `.1` and `.2` and grabbed them. A proof of `p ∨ q` carries only *one* of
the two — and we don't get to know which. So we can't project; we must **branch on the possibilities**.
That's what `cases h` does: it asks "how was this `∨` value built?" and gives us one sub-goal per answer.

- `Or` has two constructors: `Or.inl : p → p ∨ q` ("it was the left one") and `Or.inr : q → p ∨ q`
  ("the right one"). `cases h with | inl hp => … | inr hq => …` makes a branch for each, naming the
  proof it carries `hp : p` (resp. `hq : q`).
- In the `inl hp` branch we have `hp : p` and must prove `q ∨ p`. Here `p` is the *right* disjunct, so
  we build the result with `Or.inr hp`. In the `inr hq` branch, `q` is the *left* disjunct, so `Or.inl hq`.

Notice the mirroring: a value that came in on the left goes out on the right, and vice versa — exactly
what "swap" should do.

Once you trust the standard library, there's a one-liner — `Or.symm` is "commutativity of or," already
proved for you:

```lean
theorem or_swap' (p q : Prop) (h : p ∨ q) : q ∨ p := h.symm
```

Reaching for an existing lemma instead of re-deriving it is the normal way to work in Lean. But building
it by hand once, as above, is how you understand what that lemma *is*.

### Exercise 2 — `add_zero'`

```lean
theorem add_zero' (n : Nat) : n + 0 = n := rfl
```

This is the free direction. `Nat.add` is defined by `n + 0 = n` (the base equation from §6), so `n + 0`
and `n` are *the same term by definition* — even with `n` an unknown variable, because the equation
fires purely on the second argument being literally `0`. No induction, no rewriting: `rfl`. Contrast
`zero_add'` in §6, where the recursion is stuck on a variable and induction is unavoidable. Same-looking
statements, opposite difficulty — and the definition is what tells them apart.

### Exercise 3 — `succ_eq`

```lean
theorem succ_eq (n : Nat) : n + 1 = Nat.succ n := rfl
```

Also `rfl`, and unfolding *why* is satisfying. The numeral `1` is `Nat.succ 0`, so `n + 1` is really
`n + Nat.succ 0`. The step equation `n + (m+1) = (n + m) + 1` rewrites that to `Nat.succ (n + 0)`, and
`n + 0` is `n` by the base equation — so `n + 1` reduces, definitionally, all the way down to
`Nat.succ n`. The kernel performs that reduction silently, and `rfl` closes the goal. This is also why
Lean happily lets you write `n + 1` and `Nat.succ n` interchangeably: to the kernel they are *the same
number*.

> Audit your work with `#print axioms or_swap` (and the others) — each should report it depends on no
> axioms, just like the keystones in §8.
